notes.meaning: The writer opens with warm love for the Lord because God heard his cry for help. Sincere love grows out of knowing that God pays attention to our prayers in times of deep trouble. Experiencing God's deliverance stirs up true devotion and gratitude in the heart.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars note the late style of the Hebrew. They think the psalm was written after the exile, perhaps as thanks for Israel's return from Babylon, rather than by David.

notes.meaning: God leaned down his ear to listen, as a parent bends down to hear a weak child whisper. Because the Lord answered so kindly in the past, the writer promises to pray to him throughout his whole life. He commits never to turn to any other god for help.

The writer was in great pain and felt trapped by death itself. In the Old Testament, Sheol refers to the grave or the place of the dead, pictured here as ropes tying a person down. Terrible grief and fear took hold of him, leaving him feeling completely lost.

In his extreme danger, the writer called straight to the Lord for rescue. His prayer was brief, humble, and urgent, asking God to save his very life. Deep suffering taught him to pray with complete earnestness.

The Lord shows unearned favor, does what is right, and overflows with mercy. He cares deeply for his people when they hurt, like a tender father comforting his child. His willingness to deliver comes directly from this loving character.

The Lord protects the simplehearted, meaning sincere people who do not rely on clever schemes or human pride. They know they are weak and place themselves in God's hands like little children. When the writer had no strength left, God stepped in and rescued him.

The writer tells his own soul to settle down into peace once more. God is the true resting place for the human spirit, and wandering away from him brings only anxiety. Remembering how generously God has acted restores calm and confidence to the heart.

God provided a full and complete rescue from every part of his suffering. He preserved the writer's life from the grave, wiped away his bitter tears, and kept his feet from falling into ruin. Looking back on this rescue assures him of God's continuing care.

Having been spared from dying, the writer resolves to live the rest of his days under God's watchful eye. Walking before the Lord means living an honest life that pleases him, in open fellowship with him. He will use his restored life to honor God in the world of the living.

Even when severely afflicted, the writer kept his faith alive in God's promises. His confession of deep distress was made out of confidence in God, not out of total hopelessness. True trust can speak honestly about pain while still relying on the Lord.

In his sudden terror and panic, the writer thought that no human being could be trusted. He spoke in haste, feeling that everyone around him had failed him or proved unreliable. While people often let others down, God remains completely faithful to his word.

The writer asks how he could ever make a proper return to God for all his blessings. He knows he can offer nothing that could match or pay for God's incredible goodness. Real gratitude begins by realizing that we can never put God in our debt.

The writer answers his own question by lifting up the cup of salvation in public praise. In ancient worship, raising a drink offering was a sign of thanksgiving for God's rescue. The only way to repay God's kindness is to joyfully accept more of his grace and call on his name.

The writer had made solemn promises to God during his time of trouble. Now that he is saved, he pays those vows openly in front of the gathered congregation. True thankfulness is eager to testify about God's goodness in front of others.

The death of God's faithful people is of great value in his eyes. God does not allow his servants to die easily or without reason, because their lives are deeply precious to him. He watches over them constantly, even through the end of life.

Because God loosed the chains of death, the writer joyfully commits himself to be the Lord's lifelong servant. He compares himself to a houseborn slave who loves his master and chooses never to leave. God's mercy frees us so that we may gladly belong to him.

The writer prepares to offer a sacrifice of thanksgiving at the altar. Praising God from a thankful heart is an offering that truly pleases him. He joins his sacrifice with prayer, calling only on the Lord who rescued him.

The writer repeats his promise to keep his vows, naming the sacred courts of the temple in Jerusalem as the place. Joy and gratitude are not meant to stay private, but should be celebrated together with the whole community of faith. The song ends with 'Hallelujah,' inviting everyone to praise the Lord.
